transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-10-29 14:30 PT
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Dana Alvarez (CTO - Ember), Ravi Patel (Head of MLOps - Ember), Liam O'Connor (SRE - Ember)

Summary: Discovery focused on unit economics. Customer asked detailed questions about per-token costs, how batching/caching affect effective unit price, and tradeoffs for choosing Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private.

[00:00] Sofia Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick round, i'm sofia from Redwood, this is Marcus our solutions engineer. how's everyone doing?
[00:08] Dana Alvarez: Good, thanks. busy week but excited to dig in.
[00:11] Ravi Patel: Hey all. we specifically wanted to focus on costs — per token, and how we could get to something predictable for billing.
[00:18] Marcus Li: Great that's what we wanted to cover. we'll walk through typical per-token math, batching and caching levers, and then map those to Hosted / Dedicated / Private tradeoffs. Also can share a short TCO example.

[00:35] Dana Alvarez: quick context: we run a customer support summarization product. about 10k requests/day right now, avg prompt size ~120 input tokens, avg completion ~280 tokens. variability during peak up to 4x. Our infra team cares about latency under 300ms p50 for short prompts but p95 can be higher, they want cost < $Xk month but that's a ballpark.
[00:55] Marcus Li: ok helpful. so baseline tokens per request ~400 total. that's 4M tokens/day right now. what is your traffic pattern — is it steady or bursty?
[01:05] Ravi Patel: pretty bursty — lots of hourly cycles and weekday spikes.

[01:12] Sofia Chen: for framing, there are two pieces of pricing we usually discuss: raw unit compute cost (what model inference costs on GPU), and service premium (hosted infra, uptime, orchestration, ingress/egress, etc). Hosted gives fastest time to value but has a higher per-token service delta; Dedicated amortizes into reserved capacity which lowers per-token for steady high throughput; Private moves more to customer-managed ops with license/fee.

[01:38] Liam O'Connor: can you give an example with numbers? even ballpark helps us model.

[01:42] Marcus Li: sure. i'll use rough numbers as examples — exact numbers in the spreadsheet we'll send. If you average 4M tokens/day, that's ~120M tokens/month. OnHosted, assume service + model costs might be X per 1M tokens; with Dedicated, if you reserve capacity to cover baseline load you can drop effective unit cost materially because GPU utilization and fixed infra are amortized. Also batching and prefix KV caching can reduce the effective tokens you pay for compute by avoiding re-generation of common prefixes.

[02:08] Dana Alvarez: how much can batching help? our requests are short but we do have periods with lots of concurrent similar prompts.

[02:12] Marcus Li: batching depends on latency SLO and arrival distribution. for throughput-first workloads batching can improve GPU utilization and lower per-token by 20-60% in many cases. for user-facing low latency SLOs, it's more subtle: small micro-batches (2-8 requests) can still help without blowing up p95. prefix/KV cache helps when you have identical or similar prefixes — that can reduce compute for repeated tokens by up to 70% for chat-style reuse.

[02:42] Ravi Patel: you're saying caching is most effective when we have repeat conversation state or repeated system prompts? we do use a pretty long system prompt for context though.

[02:50] Marcus Li: exactly. prefix caching is great when the left context is repeated. for support summarization you might have many similar system instructions and ticket templates — caching those KV states avoids redoing attention over those tokens. if your avg prompt is 120 tokens and 60 of them are stable, you effectively only compute on the remaining 60 for many requests.

[03:10] Dana Alvarez: what about quantization? we care about model fidelity for summarization accuracy.

[03:15] Marcus Li: quantization is a tradeoff: 8-bit or 4-bit quantization can reduce memory and increase instance density on GPUs, giving better cost efficiency. Redwood's Optimize module gives recommended quant profiles per model/workload so you can test fidelity. in many summarization workloads, 4-bit int8-ish quant can be near-parity for ROUGE-style metrics but we recommend running a small eval set as part of the POC.

[03:38] Liam O'Connor: if we move to Dedicated, what are the steps and how big is the commitment?

[03:43] Sofia Chen: Dedicated is reserved GPU pools. We typically size based on target QPS and peak concurrency. commitments are monthly/annual depending on the contract; commitment levels drop unit price. You still get Redwood control plane and observability, but infra is dedicated to your tenancy. It also unlocks predictable latency and lower cold-start and warm KV cache residency.

[04:05] Dana Alvarez: what's the typical ROI timeline where Dedicated beats Hosted?

[04:09] Marcus Li: it depends on utilization. rule of thumb: if you have a steady baseline > 50% utilization of a node and predictable monthly tokens above a threshold (we gave examples in the spreadsheet), dedicated often becomes cheaper. For highly spiky, unpredictable workloads hosted with autoscaling can sometimes be more cost effective unless you can commit to a buffer.

[04:30] Ravi Patel: we plan to grow 3x in six months; may be uneven. we want to avoid overcommitting.

[04:35] Sofia Chen: one pattern we see is a hybrid: host baseline on Dedicated for predictable load and fall back to Hosted for burst capacity. Redwood supports smart routing policies that will route overflow to hosted pools or cheaper model variants automatically.

[04:50] Dana Alvarez: routing policies — are these per-route? can we say certain customers use a higher-quality model while others use a smaller model?

[04:56] Marcus Li: yes, per-route and per-customer. you can define canary or A/B routing rules, fallback policies by latency or capacity, and dedicated-to-hosted overflow. This helps control unit costs by mixing model families and capacity tiers.

[05:12] Liam O'Connor: security questions — KMS and data residency. If we go Private, how does key management work?

[05:18] Sofia Chen: Private gives you a customer-managed control plane in your VPC; KMS/HSM integrations are supported, we can use your KMS for key wrapping and we provide audit logs. We'll share our network diagram and SOC2 docs after this call.

[05:30] Ravi Patel: great. back to cost modeling — how should we think about token distribution? our internal metrics show median request ~250 tokens total, tail to 1k tokens.

[05:38] Marcus Li: when you model costs you should map your token histogram - median/mean/tail. Because per-inference cost is linear-ish with tokens, long-tail requests drive much of the cost. Techniques: response truncation with heuristics, sampling to a lower-temp smaller model for long responses, or using cascade models where a smaller model handles routine cases and the larger model is called only when needed. Redwood also supports model tiering.

[05:58] Dana Alvarez: can you show a worked example — say we have 120M tokens/month — what's the rough monthly compute in hosted vs reserved?

[06:06] Marcus Li: i'll outline a simplified worked example — again the spreadsheet has the detailed calc. Assume hosted nominal per 1M token compute + service charge = $Y. If Y is, say, $50 per 1M tokens as an example, 120M tokens -> $6k/month; with Dedicated you might amortize a node at N dollars where effective per 1M token drops to e.g. $20 per 1M at high utilization. Those are numbers for illustration only. We'll give exact pricing for the models you pick.

[06:36] Ravi Patel: that's helpful. what's the impact of batching on p95 for us? if we batch more we risk p95 spikes.

[06:43] Marcus Li: yes batching ups latency tail. Redwood's runtime supports dynamic batching with latency caps — we can set max batch size and max wait time. For user-facing latency SLOs it's common to keep micro-batches and rely on KV caching for the heavy left context. We'll run microbenchmarks during the POC to tune for your p50/p95 targets.

[07:05] Dana Alvarez: any hidden costs? egress, logging, retention?

[07:09] Sofia Chen: good question. Hosted includes typical ingress; egress and long-term retention can add costs. Observability retention beyond the included window is an add-on. For Private you'll have infrastructure costs and potentially higher operational overhead. We'll itemize those in the TCO.

[07:24] Liam O'Connor: we also do on-prem inference for some regulated customers. how different is that versus Private?

[07:30] Marcus Li: on-prem is a larger engagement — we ship an on-prem package and work with your infra team. Private with VPC is lighter since Redwood still manages the control plane but in your network. On-prem gives max isolation but requires more support and licensing costs.

[07:45] Dana Alvarez: ok sounds good. what does the POC look like — length, deliverables, benchmarks?

[07:50] Sofia Chen: typically a 4-week POC: week 0-1 setup and ingest sample prompts, week 2 benchmark runs (latency, throughput, cost per token under different batch/cache configs), week 3 evaluation on your eval set for fidelity, week 4 recommendations and handoff. Deliverables: benchmark results, TCO, config artifacts, and a POC retrospective.

[08:10] Ravi Patel: timeline wise we can kick off in mid-November if we sign off. budget for POC ~ $25k?

[08:18] Sofia Chen: that's in the expected range for a POC sized for a production-like benchmark. we'll tailor depending on scope.

[08:24] Dana Alvarez: any immediate blockers from Redwood side?

[08:27] Marcus Li: we need your sample prompt set, a test account or API key to run benchmarks, and expected token histogram and QPS targets. We'll also need who on your infra team will be the contact for networking.

[08:36] Liam O'Connor: i'll be the SRE contact. we'll share a sample dataset with redactions.

[08:40] Sofia Chen: perfect. we'll send the spreadsheet and benchmark runbook. We'll also propose a pilot architecture: baseline on a small dedicated pool + hosted overflow.

[08:48] Dana Alvarez: a couple of quick granular questions — how does Redwood account for prefix caching in billing? is cached tokens free?

[08:55] Marcus Li: billing is typically tied to inference execution. KV/prefix cache reduces compute required but billing is based on compute token equivalents executed. If a prefix is served entirely from cache and the model doesn't re-run attention over those tokens, you effectively don't pay for those cached tokens. We'll show examples in the calc; note metric definitions vary, we'll align on what you measure.

[09:20] Ravi Patel: do you have examples of customers who've cut cost by model tiering + caching?

[09:24] Sofia Chen: yes, we've seen customers reduce per token spend by 30-60% after applying caching, batching, and model tiering. we'll anonymize examples in the follow-up.

[09:33] Dana Alvarez: good, that gives us confidence. final question: what SLAs come with Dedicated?

[09:38] Sofia Chen: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets depending on contract tier. We'll include the SLA terms in commercial docs.

[09:45] Marcus Li: one operational note: Dedicated lets you pin model versions and maintain warm KV cache residency which materially helps tail latency.

[09:55] Dana Alvarez: ok let's recap and next steps.

[09:58] Sofia Chen: recap: Redwood to sendHosted vs Dedicated pricing spreadsheet, sample TCO calcs, benchmark runbook. Customer to share sample prompts, token histogram, and identify infra contact. We'll schedule a POC scoping meeting next week to finalize scope.

[10:14] Dana Alvarez: agreed. thanks everyone.

[10:17] Ravi Patel: thanks.

[10:18] Liam O'Connor: thanks.

Notes on transcription: occasional stutters and misattributed speaker labels; some technical terms transcribed as K V cache or K-V cache.
